item.title: How Trump’s Policy Agenda Runs Through One Federal Court, in Texas
item.description:
President Trump’s Justice Department had a problem. Judge after judge was rejecting its demands that hospitals across the country turn over internal records of transgender care provided to children.

By the end of April, federal judges in Boston, Philadelphia, Pittsburgh, Los Angeles and Seattle had either quashed or substantially pared back the administration’s demands that hospitals send patient records to the federal government.

But the administration did not give up. Instead, in April, it went to the Northern District of Texas’s Fort Worth courthouse, where nearly all cases go directly to the district’s chief judge, Reed O’Connor, or a second judge, Mark T. Pittman, who was appointed by Mr. Trump.

There were no hospitals in Texas that offered the transgender care at issue — state lawmakers banned gender-affirming care for minors in Texas in 2023. But the Justice Department asked the Texas court to enforce a subpoena to the Rhode Island Hospital, arguing that its nationwide investigation of such medical care was “being carried out in the Northern District of Texas.”

That was enough for Judge O’Connor, an appointee of President George W. Bush who has built a reputation as a conservative stalwart and became the district’s chief judge last August.

He granted the motion, clearing the way for the hospital to turn over a variety of personal data, including the names and Social Security numbers of minors who had received treatment.

“The subpoena’s demands are reasonable,” he wrote.

Most of the country’s 94 district courts assign cases randomly across all of their judges.

Northern Texas, where Judge O’Connor sits, does things its own way. It assigns cases to judges based on the courthouse within the district where the lawsuit is initially filed. Some courthouses are staffed by just one or two judges, meaning litigants can easily engage in “judge shopping” — filing their case in a particular courthouse and knowing to a certainty or near-certainty which judge will decide it.

In four of Northern Texas’ seven courthouses, one judge appointed by Mr. Trump hears all of the cases. In a fifth courthouse, all the cases go to Judge O’Connor. In a sixth — Fort Worth — 90 percent of the caseload is split between Judge O’Connor and Judge Pittman.

Of the district’s nine active-status judges, eight were appointed by Republican presidents — six of them by Mr. Trump. There are other districts in the country where more of the judges are Trump appointees, but very few assign cases the way Northern Texas does. And most fall outside the jurisdiction of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, widely considered to be the country’s most conservative appellate court, which hears appeals from Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi.

For years, conservative interest groups and the Texas attorney general’s office have filed lawsuits in Northern Texas, taking advantage of the district’s unusual case-assignment rules. Now, with Mr. Trump back in office, Judge O’Connor’s district has emerged as a destination for the Justice Department, as well.

A spokesman for the Justice Department declined to comment about the practice. Judge O’Connor did not respond to requests for comment.

In quick succession this year, Judge O’Connor has struck down Biden-era rules regarding ghost guns and immigration courts. He has also issued several rapid-fire orders allowing the Trump administration to reach sweeping legal settlements with opponents who appeared to actually share the federal government’s ideological goals.

Legal scholars have stressed for years that Democratic administrations and states have also availed themselves of districts with a high concentration of judges seen as more liberal. But many draw a distinction between the more prevalent practice of “forum shopping” — that is, filing in a region where groups of judges have been generally considered friendly — and that of effectively filing directly to an individual judge.

Kevin Wagner, a political science professor at Florida Atlantic University, said the precision of venue shopping in Texas was unusual, having reached the point where litigants could achieve not just a “favorable” venue but even a “predictable” one.

The administration’s efforts to get major cases with nationwide consequences in front of Judge O’Connor comes even as it condemns other judges for going beyond their remit.

Justice Department officials and Republicans in Congress have taken to calling trial court judges who exercise too much unilateral power “rogue judges.” But those criticisms from Mr. Trump’s supporters about judicial overreach are seldom aimed at judges who issue sweeping rulings that support his agenda.

Assigning major cases by geography as opposed to a random draw “undermines the appearance of impartiality,” said Nancy Gertner, a retired federal judge and a lecturer at Harvard Law School, who has been critical of the Trump administration. She said the recent attacks on the judiciary’s credibility by the political branches made it “all the more important that the standards for case assignment are fair.”

Judge O’Connor, a 61-year-old former federal prosecutor who spent time as a congressional aide before he was nominated to the bench in 2007, has emerged as a reliable skeptic of federal actions that cut against conservative orthodoxy. In 2015, he issued orders blocking paid family leave for gay couples and striking down a 1960s-era ban on interstate handgun sales.

In 2016, he struck down guidance crafted by the Obama administration directing schools to allow transgender students to use bathrooms consistent with their gender identity. In a ruling blocking the rule nationwide, he found any government guidance that included that “the definition of sex includes gender identity” to be illegal.

In 2018, Judge O’Connor invalidated the entirety of the Affordable Care Act, writing that the law amounted to an illegal tax. Even some conservative scholars described the ruling as an overreach, and the Supreme Court later voted 7 to 2 to overturn it.

In recent years, the Supreme Court has rejected other rulings from Judge O’Connor, including one limiting gun regulations, and another in which he declared that a federal law giving preference to Native American families in adoptions of Native children was unconstitutional.

Born in Texas, Judge O’Connor graduated from the University of Houston and received a law degree from the South Texas College of Law Houston in 1989.

He served nearly a decade as an assistant U.S. attorney in the Northern District of Texas, and was detailed by the Justice Department to serve as counsel to the Senate Judiciary Committee in 2003, advising Senator Orrin Hatch, Republican of Utah and the panel’s chairman. In 2005, he was sent to assist an immigration-related subcommittee, this time working under Senator John Cornyn, Republican of Texas.

“Throughout his legal career and time on the federal bench, Judge O’Connor has called balls and strikes to help preserve our independent judiciary and uphold our Constitution, and Texas is better off for it,” Senator Cornyn said in a statement.

During Judge O’Connor’s 2007 confirmation hearing, Senator Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island voiced concern about judicial nominees who he perceived to be feigning independence, only to hand down rulings in line with what he called their “political orthodoxy.”

In response, Judge O’Connor said he would follow in the path of judges who are “loyal only to the Constitution” and “call the cases as they see them.”

Judge O’Connor’s recent prominence is tied to how the Northern District of Texas assigns its cases.

Judge O’Connor now serves as the sole federal judge in Wichita Falls, Texas, hearing every case brought in that division. He also covers cases in the Fort Worth division, where for a time he was the only judge.

All cases filed in the Abilene, Lubbock and San Angelo divisions are heard by Judge James Wesley Hendrix, another Trump appointee. And yet another Trump appointee — Judge Matthew J. Kacsmaryk — handles every case in the Amarillo division. In 2023, Judge Kacsmaryk issued a well-known ruling against the legality of mifepristone, an abortion drug, after an anti-abortion group incorporated in his district a few months before filing the suit there.

Miles T. Armaly, an associate professor of political science at the University of Mississippi who coauthored a study on judge shopping in May, said the district’s power and popularity were linked to its position under the Fifth Circuit, which has upheld several of Judge O’Connor’s most contested rulings.

Even so, the circuit has jumped ahead of the Supreme Court in scrutinizing others, including rulings on Biden-era pistol brace regulations and a dispute between Elon Musk’s social media platform X and the liberal watchdog organization Media Matters.

Even after the Supreme Court’s decision last year curtailing the power of individual judges to block federal policies nationwide, Mr. Armaly said, single-judge divisions remain an important tool for litigants with political goals that extend outside the district.

The new limitations on nationwide injunctions took “one of the tools out of the tool kit,” he said, “but the construction project is still the same.”

Particularly under the second Trump administration, the Fifth Circuit has also emerged as a pipeline of contested decisions that the Supreme Court has increasingly been forced to untangle. It also stands out as the most reversed appeals court.

Alexander Gouzoules, an associate professor at the at the University of Missouri School of Law, said the combination of factors in Texas that allows litigants to choose a judge with known views and survive an appeal has increasingly encouraged people seeking an “outlier result” to file there over the past decade.

“Any one of these problems might be solvable on its own,” he said. “But when they’re combined with each other, there is a sort of exponential effect on the kind of destabilizing outcomes it produces.”

Single-judge divisions have sparked bipartisan complaints.

In 2021, a report on patent filings noted that litigants were funneling 20 percent of all patent lawsuits nationwide to a single judge in the Western District of Texas. The study prompted Senator Thom Tillis, Republican of North Carolina, and Senator Patrick Leahy, Democrat of Vermont, to write a letter demanding a review; their concerns were later cited by Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr.

Complaints grew so loud that in March 2024, the Judicial Conference of the United States, the administrative and policy-making arm of the federal judiciary, adopted new, nonbinding policy guidance advising judicial districts to randomly assign cases when major federal policies with nationwide implications were at stake.

“The random case-assignment policy deters judge shopping,” said Judge Robert J. Conrad Jr., who heads the federal courts’ Administrative Office, in an announcement. “It promotes the impartiality of proceedings and bolsters public confidence in the federal judiciary.”

The proposed changes were not well received in Texas.

Two weeks later, the Northern District’s chief judge at the time, David C. Godbey, announced that the judges of the district had met and decided not to adopt the change.

Judge O’Connor added his voice later that year, denouncing the Judicial Conference’s recommendation as an attack on his district, in a speech to the conservative Federalist Society.

He complained that the conference’s comments were hypocritical, criticizing the Justice Department under President Joseph R. Biden Jr. as “a frequent forum shopper.” And he lamented the Judicial Conference’s decision as bowing to “external political criticism” from “so-called commentators and elected political officials” that he said were intent on “undermining the judiciary.”

“Make no mistake about it: This pressure remains,” he said. “It remains a constant source of pressure and will not ease up any time soon.”

With Mr. Trump’s return to the White House, the administration has repeatedly filed crucial matters in Judge O’Connor’s divisions.

Last summer, the Justice Department sued Texas in Wichita Falls, where Judge O’Connor handles every case. The lawsuit challenged a first-of-its-kind Texas law that granted in-state tuition to undocumented students. Texas lawmakers had in recent years tried unsuccessfully to repeal the statute, which was adopted on a bipartisan basis in 2011.

Instead, Ken Paxton, the Republican Texas attorney general and a close ally of Mr. Trump, made no effort to defend the law, instead working with the Justice Department to draw up a hasty legal agreement to strike it down. Outside groups argued that the proposed agreement was an abuse of the court system because the federal government and the state of Texas were on the same side.

But Judge O’Connor approved the settlement the same day, accepting a contested view that the two-decade-old law was “invalid.” The Fifth Circuit last year declined to block the settlement, but has not yet issued a final ruling on an appeal filed by a group of individuals and nonprofits.

The two sides swapped roles this year when Mr. Paxton, who is running for Senate in Texas with Mr. Trump’s endorsement, sued the federal government in Wichita Falls in June over a 2024 Biden-era rule that allows immigration judges to suspend some deportation proceedings. America First Legal, a group co-founded by Stephen Miller, a senior White House adviser and the architect of much of Mr. Trump’s immigration policy, helped represent Texas.

Again, the two sides were ideologically aligned but formally on opposite sides in a lawsuit. Together, they presented an agreement that removed immigration judges’ discretion to block deportations under certain circumstances. On the same day the lawsuit was filed, Judge O’Connor signed off on the settlement with a brief order.

In the case of the hospital subpoena, a Rhode Island state agency filed a new suit asking the federal court in Rhode Island to halt the out-of-state demands from Texas.

After considering the chain of events, Judge Mary McElroy, a Federal District Court judge in Rhode Island, upbraided the Justice Department, accusing its lawyers of a “crusade to obtain transgender children’s medical records,” and of fleeing her court “in favor of a distant forum that D.O.J. deems friendly to its political positions.”

During a hearing, she described the tactic of “shopping” the case to Texas as “dirty pool” and granted a motion to quash the subpoenas.

The Justice Department told her it had good reason to base the investigation in North Texas. In May, Judge O’Connor ruled it was “necessary and prudent” for Rhode Island Hospital to turn over the documents to him personally, in case the Justice Department ultimately prevails at the conclusion of the complicated litigation.

An appeals court for Rhode Island has deferred to Judge O’Connor, for now. Oral arguments in the appellate case are scheduled for October. In the meantime, the hospital has begun turning over records, which it noted would take “a period of months.”

Engineering that outcome, in Judge McElroy’s view, is why the Justice Department took the case to Northern Texas in the first place.

“You chose Judge O’Connor in Texas,” she told a Justice Department attorney in court in May. “Let’s just admit that.”

item.title: This Governor Could Lose His Primary. A Bridge May Be to Blame.
item.description:
The abrupt closure of a crucial Rhode Island bridge in 2023 has cast a long shadow in the small state, driving traffic delays and fueling fury ever since.

It is also providing a dramatic backdrop for a close and heated primary showdown between Gov. Dan McKee, a Democrat seeking a second term, and Helena Foulkes, a former CVS executive who has sharply criticized the governor’s handling of the bridge saga.

Mr. McKee, 75, a former mayor and lieutenant governor, first assumed his post in 2021 when his predecessor, Gina Raimondo, was tapped by President Joseph R. Biden Jr. to be the U.S. commerce secretary. He says that when an engineer revealed critical structural failures that could have caused the Washington Bridge in Providence to collapse, he took decisive action, putting public safety above his political future.

Ms. Foulkes, 62, who led the retail division at CVS, has alleged that the governor hid information about the bridge’s closure from the public, protected allies who should have been immediately fired once the structure’s risks were revealed, and added to costs and delays with politically driven decisions.

The governor has forcefully denied those claims and sought to turn voters’ attention to Ms. Foulkes’s leadership at CVS, asserting that she failed to do enough to stop the pharmacy chain from fueling the opioid addiction crisis. CVS agreed to pay $5 billion in 2022 to settle lawsuits over its role.

The race between the two Democrats is a replay of the primary in 2022, a year before the bridge was closed, when Mr. McKee barely eked out a win against Ms. Foulkes. This time, though, Mr. McKee is facing not just anger about the bridge, but a tide of national anti-incumbent sentiment.

A poll conducted this month by Emerson College showed Ms. Foulkes leading in their rematch by 15 points.

Experts said the race was likely to tighten as the primary, scheduled for Sept. 9, draws near. But Adam Myers, a political scientist at Providence College, said Ms. Foulkes’s apparent lead did not surprise him, given her strong showing four years ago and — fairly or unfairly — some voters’ inclination to blame Mr. McKee for the bridge closure and resulting traffic chaos.

Mr. McKee has maintained that his decisions regarding the bridge, which links Providence to its eastern suburbs, as well as to southeastern Massachusetts and Cape Cod, have been driven solely by the state’s best interest.

“I know there is a lot of frustration, and I accept it,” he said in an interview. “But in the end, people are going to realize we did the right thing.”

The state leans heavily Democratic; its last Republican governor left office in 2011. In the Republican primary, Elaine Pelino, a first-time candidate who describes herself as fully aligned with President Trump, has maintained a strong lead over Aaron Guckian, who ran unsuccessfully for lieutenant governor in 2022 and is more of a moderate.

The bridge drama began almost three years ago, when an engineer noticed irregularities. The subsequent discovery of critical failures in the 60-year-old westbound side of the bridge prompted its immediate closure; soon after, the state announced that it would be demolished and rebuilt, while the eastbound span was reconfigured to carry two-way traffic over the Seekonk River.

Mr. McKee faced criticism for keeping on the state’s transportation chief for more than two years after the closure. The state has sued more than a dozen companies that previously worked on the bridge, blaming them for failing to address its problems. The companies have argued in court that the state bore ultimate responsibility.

Mr. McKee stresses recent progress on the project, pointing to a $342 million federal investment in the work and describing it as ahead of schedule. . Demolition of the old bridge is complete and construction is underway on the substructure of the new bridge, scheduled for completion in 2028.

But voters like Artie Souza, 74, have yet to move on. Mr. Souza, a former Democrat who recently changed his status to unenrolled, and a retired truck driver from East Providence who commuted daily over the bridge, said he probably would have voted for Mr. McKee if not for the disruption.

“I’ll be nice and call it a fiasco,” he said. “Thank God I retired the year before. It took too long to fix, and he could have done better. He would be low on my list right now.”

Mr. McKee has emphasized his attention to working-class concerns, describing a record of new job creation and bigger investments in public education. His campaign has also emphasized Ms. Foulkes’s wealth and corporate ties, calling her an elitist who wants to “buy” the election. She ran the retail division at CVS, with 200,000 employees, from 2014 to 2018.

“I’m the governor for the people, and she’s the governor for corporate interests,” he said in an interview. “This is a very winnable race — the people know I’m one of them.”

Ms. Foulkes’s uncle is former Senator Chris Dodd, a Democrat from Connecticut; Nancy Pelosi, the former House speaker, was her mother’s college roommate and is scheduled to appear at a rally with Ms. Foulkes in Providence on Sunday.

Ms. Foulkes has defended her record as a corporate leader. In a recent interview, she said CVS cut its dispersal of opioids by almost 40 percent during her tenure. She also criticized Mr. McKee for attacking her former employer, which is the largest corporation headquartered in Rhode Island. “People are upset he’s going to drive CVS away,” she said.

But Rhonda Pimentel, 61, an unenrolled voter from East Providence, was more upset by the possibility that Ms. Foulkes could have done more to stem the opioid crisis, which hit New England hard in the mid-2010s.

“I don’t like it,” Ms. Pimentel said. “I didn’t like it when it happened.”

Parked outside a supermarket after shopping, she said that she would reluctantly vote for Mr. McKee, despite her desire for “new blood,” because she did not feel that she could trust Ms. Foulkes.

Tony Soares, 57, an unenrolled voter from Providence, said he supported Ms. Foulkes because he thought she would get things done.

Standing on the riverfront in East Providence, where cranes towered over the bridge construction site and two-way traffic flowed steadily over the eastbound span, Mr. Soares said he did not blame Mr. McKee for the bridge’s failure.

Still, he said, it felt as if the governor should go.

“I think we’re in a time when everyone wants a change, a disruption,” Mr. Soares said. “She’s that disruption.”

item.title: Most Democrats Don’t Want to Talk About Transgender Athletes. He’s Leaning In.
item.description:
Senator Ed Markey of Massachusetts might be the only high-profile Democrat in America eagerly campaigning as a supporter of transgender rights.

Even as many other top Democrats have grown cagey on the issue, Mr. Markey is offering a passionate defense of transgender athletes as he runs in a primary contest on Tuesday against Representative Seth Moulton, a more moderate challenger.

Mr. Markey has argued in particular that Mr. Moulton “threw trans kids under the bus” when, shortly after the 2024 election, the congressman attributed Democrats’ defeat in part to their position on transgender issues. Mr. Moulton long defended his remarks but expressed some contrition for them this month.

“Trans athletes should be able to play,” Mr. Markey said in an interview this past week. “That reflects Massachusetts and who we are. And Seth Moulton does not.”

Mr. Markey, 80, has staked out his ardent pro-trans rights position at a moment when the rest of his party is grappling with the issue, which President Trump and other Republicans have used as a cultural wedge. Ambitious younger Democrats who are likely to run for president — including Gov. Gavin Newsom of California and Pete Buttigieg, the former transportation secretary — have edged away from defending the participation of transgender athletes in women’s and girls’ sports.

Other prominent Democrats have sought to defuse the issue by not talking about it or punting responsibility while trying to pivot to more favorable issues like the economy.

Mr. Markey has leaned in. He is, according to Charlotte Clymer, a liberal activist and strategist who is transgender and supports the senator, “the only one who is really talking about this front and center.”

Mr. Markey said that transgender rights had “become a defining issue in this race because Massachusetts voters believe it’s disqualifying if you don’t stand up for human rights everywhere and all the time,” adding, “I believe you can be right, but too soon.”

The senator’s forceful message on trans rights has been fueled by the comments made by Mr. Moulton, who had largely been seen as an ally of L.G.B.T.Q. groups, the day after the 2024 election.

“Democrats spend way too much time trying not to offend anyone rather than being brutally honest about the challenges many Americans face,” Mr. Moulton told The New York Times. “I have two little girls, I don’t want them getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete, but as a Democrat I’m supposed to be afraid to say that.”

There was an immediate backlash.

Mr. Moulton’s campaign manager resigned. A city councilor in his hometown hosted a rally in opposition. Mr. Moulton defended his remarks and clashed on the issue with Gov. Maura Healey, the state’s first L.G.B.T.Q. governor. He wrote an opinion essay for The Washington Post under the headline, “I’m done with Democratic purity tests.”

The drama cemented Mr. Moulton’s image as a Democrat willing to buck his own party. He first came to Congress after ousting a longtime incumbent in 2014. Four years later, he led a group of House Democrats who tried and failed to block Representative Nancy Pelosi from becoming House speaker.

So when Mr. Moulton, 47, entered the Senate race last year, he argued that Mr. Markey was too old to seek another six years in Washington — especially when Democrats are still haunted by President Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s failed re-election bid. Mr. Markey and his allies made Mr. Moulton’s remarks about trans rights a centerpiece of their attacks against him.

Mr. Moulton has since cosponsored congressional legislation known as the transgender bill of rights, of which Mr. Markey is the original author. At a debate this month, Mr. Moulton also issued a qualified apology for his comments after the 2024 election.

“I deeply recognize your trauma,” he said, addressing “the trans community feeling the weight and the pain” of the Trump administration’s policies. “And I’m sorry if my comments hurt you.”

In an interview last week, Mr. Moulton said that despite that apology, he was not sorry for the substance of his earlier remarks. He said that Democrats should acknowledge that voters do not want a full integration of trans athletes into youth sports.

“There are a lot of people who agree with Democrats that trans people should be protected, have full rights, and should be able to serve in the military,” he said. “But when it comes to competitive sports, they feel uncomfortable. And our party’s message to those people has been: You are wrong and you’re a terrible person.”

He blamed Mr. Markey for injecting a divisive social issue into the primary campaign.

“Markey has tried to weaponize this issue and trans people, using them as a political football to divide voters just like the Republicans are,” Mr. Moulton said.

When asked to name the highest-profile transgender person supporting his campaign, he demurred.

“I don’t know how to answer that question, exactly,” he said. “I know there’s a number of trans people who are involved.”

Dallas Ducar, a Markey supporter who founded a transgender health care clinic in Northampton, Mass., said the senator’s position on trans rights was a signal that he was the progressive in the race.

“He is speaking to the around 70-plus percent of Democrats that know and understand that trans people are morally legitimate and deserving of their civil rights,” said Ms. Ducar, who is transgender. “If people were asking the same question about civil rights in the 1960s and ’70s, I’d want to be on the side of the progressives.”

The available polling suggests Mr. Markey is favored in the primary race. Even Mr. Moulton acknowledged that he was behind, but he said he was counting on a comeback in the campaign’s final days.

The winner of the primary will be a heavy favorite in the general election in deep-blue Massachusetts.

Mr. Moulton urged Massachusetts Democrats to think beyond their state lines. He said the state should elect a senator who could appeal to the rest of the country to help the party build a governing majority in Washington.

He argued that it would not advance the progressive cause to have the Democratic Party branded as enthusiastically supportive of trans athletes in sports, when polls suggest that the American public believes differently.

“We need to think more about the entire Democratic team, because we’re in the minority,” Mr. Moulton said. “A lot of politics has become a purity test these days, but I’m not sure that’s good for the party or the country. We’re a democracy. We should be able to have discussions.”

item.title: Postal Service Rule Could Bar Millions From Voting By Mail
item.description:
Voting by mail would become much more difficult, if not impossible, for tens of millions of Americans if the U.S. Postal Service is allowed to implement a restrictive rule governing mail voting that President Trump has demanded.

The effects would likely be greater for Democratic voters, who vote by mail in higher numbers than Republicans, and in states where mail voting is universal or nearly so. Mail voting may not happen at all in states that resist the Trump administration’s demands for voter data.

The rule would particularly affect people in rural areas and older voters, who tend to cast ballots by mail in greater numbers. It could also deeply affect states where some of the most competitive races for House, Senate and governor will determine control of Congress and state governments.

Michigan, where 37 percent of votes were cast by mail in 2022, would be one epicenter, with hard-fought statewide contests and multiple battleground House races. California, which mails ballots to all voters, is expected to be central to Democratic efforts to win a majority in the House.

The rule is being challenged in several lawsuits, and it is on hold temporarily following a federal judge’s ruling on Thursday. The administration is appealing. Even if the Postal Service is permitted to proceed, it is unclear that it would have time to implement the plan ahead of an election that is fewer than 70 days away.

For instance, the rule requires states to upload a list of voters to a federal mail ballot portal that is not yet online. Nearly two dozen Democratic-led states and Washington, D.C., have sued to block the proposed rule and said they will not comply with it.

If the agency were to move ahead, state and local officials would shoulder enormous costs in what would need to be a herculean effort to prepare election offices and educate voters in time for the midterm elections in November.

The most dramatic aspect of the proposed rule is a plan to deny services for election mail entirely in states that do not turn over voter data, which federal officials say they want to use to identify noncitizens on state voter rolls. The policy would upend mail voting in any state that does not comply, but the effects would be measurably greater in the smaller number of states that rely heavily on mail voting.

More than one in three Democrats voted by mail in 2024, compared with about one in four Republicans, according to estimates by the States United Democracy Center, which examined voting data in 32 states where it was available.

“It’s not that complicated,” said Marc Elias, the Democratic election lawyer, who said the new policy was a blatant effort to disenfranchise Democrats. “The administration knows that Democrats are more likely to vote by mail than Republicans. Donald Trump has demonized voting by mail and made that differential even greater.”

It is far from certain that the rule could be implemented this year, given outstanding legal and logistical challenges with fewer than 10 weeks before Election Day. North Carolina, where a highly competitive Senate race could help determine control of the chamber, is set to mail ballots to some voters starting next week. More states will soon follow.

President Trump, who voted by mail himself in Florida’s primary this month, created the current uncertainty by signing an executive order in March that called on the Department of Homeland Security to compile state-by-state citizenship lists that could be used to help determine voter eligibility.

Last week, the Supreme Court ruled that the lawsuit was premature because the Postal Service had not yet finalized its rule. Now that the agency has done so, though, and a lower court has weighed in, the justices will likely be asked to rule again in the coming weeks, this time on the constitutionality of the plan.

Elections officials from both parties have said that forcing the counties and municipalities that run the nation’s elections to implement new rules in such a short time frame would inject chaos into the nation’s voting processes and could halt mail voting altogether.

Small-town clerks would have to purchase new machines to print the bar codes required under the new rule. All mail ballots — including some that in the past may have been hand-delivered from a local elections official to the local post office — would now have to be routed through a big-city mail sorting center, since only major hubs are able to process the new bar codes.

“People need to understand the changing of an election is somewhat like changing the course of an aircraft carrier. You can’t do it on short notice,” said Alan Hays, a supervisor of elections and a Republican in Lake County, Fla., where Mr. Trump received 62 percent of the vote in 2024. “Putting such an awesome responsibility on the U.S. Postal Service, with the track record that organization has, on such a short notice is unwise at best.”

The effects would vary across jurisdictions.

In Wisconsin, throwing a wrench into mail voting would cause far more chaos in the state’s rural communities than in its more liberal cities, said Ann Jacobs, a Democratic member of the Wisconsin Elections Commission.

Cities would be able to extend in-person early-voting hours to accommodate a decrease in mail voting, while the state’s far-flung townships would likely have fewer resources and staff to extend voting hours.

“We have clerks who are running the elections out of their homes until Election Day,” Ms. Jacobs said.

No state in the country is home to more critical elections this year or a wider partisan gap in mail voting than Michigan.

The state will administer one of the nation’s most competitive Senate races, a contest that is critical to Democratic hopes of taking back control of the chamber. It also has what is expected to be hard-fought, open-seat elections for governor and other statewide offices, along with four battleground House races. Majority control of both chambers of the narrowly divided Michigan Legislature is also up for grabs.

Nearly 2 million Michiganders are now on the state’s permanent mail voting list, meaning that each election, officials automatically mail them ballots. And while Michigan voters do not register by party, there is a sizable gap between the number of votes for Democratic candidates and those for Republicans that are processed by mail, according to an analysis by the MIT Election Data and Science Lab.

In the last midterm election in 2022, about 57 percent of ballots cast for Democrats arrived by mail, compared with just 37 percent ballots cast for Republicans, MIT found. The gap was more pronounced in 2024, when Mr. Trump was on the ballot and regularly denounced mail voting on the campaign trail. That year, 60 percent of votes for then-Vice President Kamala Harris arrived by mail, compared with 34 percent of votes for Mr. Trump.

“Anything that obstructs a voter’s ability to vote hurts Democrats in Michigan,” said Lon Johnson, a former chairman of the Michigan Democratic Party. “The more complications you have, the more people become suspect, the more they fall into Trump’s line of argument that voting and democracy is a system can be rigged.”

Jim Runestad, a state senator and the chairman of the Michigan Republican Party, said he was not aware of any discussions with Republican campaigns in the state about how they might alter their get-out-the-vote strategy if the rules on mail ballots changed before Election Day.

Mr. Runestad, who said he receives his ballot in the mail and typically returns it to his municipal clerk’s office, said he would prefer that people be required to vote in person on Election Day.

“I know that Republicans are more and more turning to mail-in voting in much larger numbers than they ever have before,” he said. “What ought to be of concern across the board for everyone is to make sure that there is no mischief.”

The effects could also be profound in the eight states, as well as Washington, D.C., that mail ballots to all voters. Washington State has done away with in-person voting entirely. Once voters receive their ballots in the mail, they can either deposit them in a drop box, drop them at a voting center or send them back through the Postal Service.

Even in states that still offer polling locations, Mr. Trump’s rules could foment chaos for election administrators who have built systems around mail balloting. Confusion is likely among voters who have not visited a polling place in years.

In Arizona, where about 80 percent of voters received mail ballots in the last midterm election in 2022, Adrian Fontes, the secretary of state, said he was planning for as much as 85 percent this year. Mr. Fontes, a Democrat, predicted that restricting mail voting in Arizona would create a backlash from Republican retirees who have long voted by mail.

The MIT analysis found that an estimated 62 percent of Arizona Republicans voted by mail in 2024, compared with 75 percent of Democrats.

“Arizona would no longer be a battleground state,” said Mr. Fontes, who is up for re-election this year. “It would turn deep, dark blue. Mail voting was created by Republicans, promoted by Republicans, advanced by Republicans and that’s how Republican voters like to vote. You think they want that convenience and that security taken away from them? Hell no.”

item.title: Dolly Parton Was Shaped by a Small Rural Church. They’re Fading Away.
item.description:
For years, Mary Berry attended a small Baptist church in the rural Kentucky community where her family has lived and farmed for generations.

She taught Sunday school. She brought food to hundreds of potlucks. At one point she served as a deacon alongside a janitor, a tenant farmer, and the community’s doctor. Everyone knew everyone, and if differences of opinion were sensed, they were not discussed.

As the local economy suffered in the early 2000s, however, so did the congregation. Disputes arose over cultural and political topics that had never been at issue before. A pastor was ousted over his stance on same-sex marriage. Ms. Berry left, too.

“As I got older and began to see the loss of the cohesive agrarian culture I grew up in, I began to see what we were really losing was that sort of gathering where all kinds of people gathered as equals,” Ms. Berry, the daughter of the poet and farmer Wendell Berry, recalled this week. “It wasn’t perfect, but it was pretty darn good.”

She was speaking days after the death of Dolly Parton, a woman who was also shaped by a small rural church in Appalachia.

Since her death in Nashville last week at the age of 80, tributes have poured in from conservative Southern Baptists and progressive Unitarians, from twice-on-Sunday churchgoers to people who avoid institutions altogether.

What many of them seemed to be mourning was not just Ms. Parton as a performer, but as a Christian who represented for many an idealized style of faith, and in particular, Southern or Appalachian faith: folksy and unpretentious, oriented around Jesus and rollicking old-time music, and centered in small rural congregations that prize community over ideology.

Those small churches “are very place-based, deeply rooted institutions” said Jessie Wilkerson, a professor at the University of Tennessee in Knoxville and a historian of Appalachia.

Ms. Parton’s lifetime saw the rise of megachurches, which have replaced many more intimate congregations like the one she was born into. About one in three Protestant churchgoers now attends a church that attracts at least 1,000 people on a weekend, according to the Hartford Institute for Religion Research.

Those large churches, including those anchored by a central congregation that plants multiple campuses throughout a region, have damaged many independent congregations with fewer resources.

Ms. Parton’s grandfather was the pastor of the House of Prayer, a small Pentecostal church in Sevier County, Tenn. She was singing in the choir by age 6, and was baptized in the Little Pigeon River at 12. Her faith has infused countless songs, even as she wrestled with the occasional contradictions between what she called her “three passions”: God, music and sex.

“Rural southern Christianity, especially at that time, seemed much warmer than what we see in American life now,” said Russell Moore, an editor at large and columnist at Christianity Today magazine, who was raised in a Baptist church in rural Mississippi and now lives in Nashville. “You actually did have people in community, meaning people knew when someone was sick, and could bear with other people’s failings.”

But he cautioned against idealizing the era. “The shadow side of that was often propping up horrific sin, such as what we see in Jim Crow racial oppression,” he said. “We can’t talk about one without seeing the other.”

More scholarship is needed about the role of small churches in the racial conflicts of the 20th century, said Anthea Butler, an emerita professor at the University of Pennsylvania who studies race and American religion. In her view, the widespread nostalgia for a Dolly-style Christianity is primarily about the experience of belonging to any kind of close-knit church that offers deep relationships and sets the rhythms of the week.

“People have forgotten all these hymns, people don’t think about having Sunday dinner after church, these communal activities in spaces that are small but feel homey,” she said. “All we see are big church things, big church scandals.”

In South Carolina, Alphaeus Anderson was leading the University of South Carolina Upstate Gospel Choir in a performance of Ms. Parton’s classic “9 to 5” on Tuesday when the singers noticed people in the audience checking their phones with urgency. The news was breaking that Ms. Parton had died.

The coincidence had Mr. Anderson thinking about his own upbringing playing gospel music at First Baptist Church of Fairforest, S.C., a Black congregation where the pastor was also a powerful gospel singer, and prayer often blended into music.

Mr. Anderson’s parents still attend the church, and he visits on holidays. But the congregation has gotten much smaller and older over the years.

“No youth, no church,” he said. “A few more birthdays, and not just my home church but the rich legacy they’ve instilled in us will disappear with them.”

Like many Americans, Ms. Parton came to describe herself as spiritual but “not that religious.” As an adult, she was not known to attend public services regularly.

About 45 percent of white Southerners who identify as Protestant go to church no more than once a year, according to an analysis of 2018 data from the General Social Survey by Daniel K. Williams, a historian at Ashland University in Ohio. Gallup found that churchgoing by Black adults dropped by almost 20 points between 2000 and 2020.

“In the Bible Belt, churchgoing is important, but faith, and especially evangelical faith, transcends church boundaries,” Mr. Williams said.

Despite her move away from organized religion, the archetype of the country church remained a touchstone for Ms. Parton — one she felt wistful enough about to build a version for her fans. She oversaw the installation of a one-room chapel on the grounds of Dollywood, her flagship amusement park in Pigeon Forge, Tenn. A staff chaplain presides over Sunday services.

For Silas House, a novelist who grew up in a congregation in eastern Kentucky about 90 minutes from Ms. Parton’s hometown, the small rural church of his childhood was a paradoxical institution. Its members taught him the “radical empathy” of Jesus, he said. But he also knew from a young age that if they knew he was gay, that empathy could be withdrawn.

Ms. Parton’s public persona as someone who consistently embraced gay people and was also “quite Jesus-y” was a balm to him in later years when he didn’t feel comfortable attending church.

“For a lot of people including myself, Dolly became what we wanted out of Christianity,” Mr. House said. “She was one of the people who allowed me to come out, and one of the people who allowed me to retain my faith.”

Over the years, many Christian denominations and individual churches and believers have moved to embrace gay people. Mr. House is now an active member of an Episcopal congregation in Lexington that sponsors the city’s Pride parade.

In 2018, he published a novel about an evangelical pastor in Nashville who faces a reckoning as he begins to shift his opposition to homosexuality. He got a letter in the mail from Ms. Parton, addressed to him and his mentor: “It’s a wonderful and much needed story,” she wrote. “God bless you both.”

item.title: ‘Freedom Fuel’ Touts Cheap Gas. A Suit Says the Dealer Didn’t Pay for It.
item.description:
Last month the Trump administration promoted a chain of gas stations that were lowering prices in the Northeast because “they love the U.S.A.” Now, a new lawsuit claims that some of the fuel sold by the gas stations came from a dealer that never paid for it.

The chain of gas stations, called the Freedom Fuel Network, had lowered gas prices at 25 stations in the Philadelphia area, President Trump said in July. But a lawsuit filed this month in federal court claims that the Freedom Fuel Network was able to sell its gas at lower prices because some of the fuel derived from a dealer that had not paid for the gas.

The lawsuit was filed by the Georgia-based Mansfield Energy against KRSM, a company based in New Jersey, and its president, Syed Kazmi. From May 21 to July 7, KRSM picked up 1.1 million gallons of fuel worth nearly $4 million from a fuel supply terminal in Pennsylvania, the suit claims.

Then, KRSM sold that fuel to gas stations that were part of the Freedom Fuel Network, which was able to sell gas at lower prices than its competitors did, the lawsuit claims.

“KRSM was able to sell such fuel for such low prices and garner such publicity because it never paid plaintiff for such fuel,” the lawsuit says.

Urs Broderick Furrer, a lawyer representing Mansfield, said in a statement that Mr. Kazmi had picked up the fuel from Mansfield’s account.

“Despite the fact that the last delivery was more than five weeks ago, KRSM has not paid one dollar towards the $4,000,000 that KRSM owes Mansfield,” Mr. Furrer said. Some of that gas, Mr. Furrer said, was delivered to at least 10 locations that are listed on Freedom Fuel Network’s website. The lawsuit does not name the Freedom Fuel Network as a defendant, and does not detail how much of the unpaid fuel was received from KRSM.

Mauro Tucci, a lawyer representing Mr. Kazmi, said in an email, “KRSM disputes the allegations in this case, which is an accounting dispute over fuel invoices mis-priced by Mansfield Oil.”

According to the lawsuit, because of a data error, Mansfield did not receive information it needed to send invoices to KRSM until early July. After some discrepancies with invoices, the lawsuit says, Mansfield submitted draft requests to KRSM’s account in late July and was later told by its bank that KRSM had refused the drafts.

During phone calls with Mansfield between late July and early August, Mr. Kazmi said that KRSM would pay for the fuel, but payment had yet to be received, the lawsuit claims.

The lawsuit does not detail how Mr. Kazmi was connected to the Freedom Fuel Network or who owns it. A trademark application filed with the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office in July does not name owners for the Freedom Fuel Network.

“The Administration has had zero contact or dealings with the defendant: KRSM Inc or Sayed Kazmi,” a White House spokesperson said.

President Trump said in a post on Truth Social on July 1 that gas prices were falling, but “not as fast as they should be.” Ahead of the July 4 holiday, the Freedom Fuel Network planned to lower gas prices at 25 stations across the Greater Philadelphia area, Mr. Trump said.

“This Retailer is taking the lead, and others should follow,” Mr. Trump said. “They are doing this because they love the U.S.A.”

The Trump administration did not provide additional explanation for why gas stations in the Freedom Fuel Network were able to sell gas at a lower cost. On July 7, the White House posted a video on social media at a Freedom Fuel Network gas station that sold gas for $3.47 per gallon in Philadelphia, where the cost of a gallon of gas reached $3.99 that week.

Less than two weeks later, the national average for a gallon of gas reached $4, as the war with Iran rekindled. Yesterday, the national average for a gallon of gas was $4.08, according to the AAA motor club.

item.title: Why the United States Can’t Quit Its Wars
item.description:
For much of the Afghanistan war, the only thing harder for the United States than winning was quitting.

The country’s longest war ended in chaos and defeat five years ago Sunday. Hundreds of thousands of Afghans, desperate to escape Taliban insurgents, swarmed the Kabul airport. Thirteen U.S. troops died there in a suicide bombing.

But since then, the fears that prevented three presidents from quitting the war have proven to be unfounded. Afghanistan has not become a terror haven or launchpad for attacks in the United States.

Today, the U.S. military is mired in a new war in Iran. Once again, the prospects for a military victory look bleak. Even President Trump has hinted that he would like to quit the war, only to reverse course and make a case for staying.

“We don’t have to be there,” he said in an Oval Office address in the spring. “We don’t need their oil. We don’t need anything they have. But we’re there to help our allies.”

The long war in Afghanistan raises hard questions for the generals and policymakers contemplating the way forward in Iran: Why was quitting in Afghanistan so hard? What does the long struggle to accept defeat there say about the Trump administration’s predicament in Iran?

The United States has faced questions about quitting in just about every war it has fought since its emergence as a global power after World War II. “So much of what we’ve been involved in these last several decades is really policing the empire,” said Andrew R. Hoehn, a senior analyst at RAND Corporation, a think tank that studies security matters.

In most instances, U.S. troops have gone to war to impose order on an unruly world, or to defend American values. “We’re not fighting existential conflicts,” Mr. Hoehn said.

The aftermath of Osama bin Laden’s death in May 2011 offered the best opportunity to leave Afghanistan. The perpetrator of the Sept. 11 terror attacks was dead, and a decade of drone strikes had decimated his organization. The Taliban insurgents, who had ruled Afghanistan and harbored Al Qaeda before the U.S. invasion, were proving almost impossible to eradicate.

“If American officials had know then what they know now, many of them — including me — would have argued more strongly for an early withdrawal,” Carter Malkasian, who advised U.S. commanders in Afghanistan, recently wrote in an essay in Foreign Affairs magazine.

Presidents and the Pentagon were motivated to keep fighting by concerns about the country’s credibility, a sense of obligation to trusted Afghan allies and a feeling that defeat would dishonor the sacrifices made by dead and wounded troops.

For many of these officers, who lost close friends in firefights with the Taliban, the idea of quitting ran counter to years of training and experience.

“Simply put, one reason the Americans did not leave Afghanistan earlier is that the U.S. military fights to win,” Mr. Malkasian wrote.

Political and foreign policy leaders fretted about U.S. credibility on the world stage and the costs that they could pay at the ballot box for losing a war.

By 2011, U.S. troop levels had already begun falling in Afghanistan, and the Taliban recognized that it just needed to outlast U.S. troops and the exhausted American public’s willingness to pay for the war.

As the prospect of defeating the Taliban grew more remote, U.S. political leaders shifted their goals. They focused on reducing casualties, cutting the war’s costs and keeping the corrupt and unpopular Afghan government alive.

“They’re like a doctor in a critical care ward that knows the patient is going to die,” said Rosemary Kelanic, the Middle East program director at Defense Priorities, which promotes a more modest U.S. foreign policy. “They’re just hoping the patient dies after their shift is over. They don’t want it to be on their watch.”

The war continued for another decade after bin Laden’s death, claiming the lives of another 868 service members. U.S. commanders who led troops in the war’s waning years sensed that they were being set up to fail. On a recent podcast, Gen. Austin S. Miller, the last commander in Afghanistan, recalled his mind-set when he was selected in 2018 for the job. He expected to emerge from his tour “very tired” and with a “diminished reputation.”

His situation, he joked darkly, was best summed up by song lyrics from the rock band Steely Dan: “I’m a fool to do your dirty work.”

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth vowed earlier this year that the war in Iran would be nothing like the long wars in Afghanistan and Iraq. Mr. Hegseth had deployed to both conflicts as a young Army National Guard officer. The experience left him angry and disillusioned.

“Hear it from me, one of hundreds of thousands who fought in Iraq and Afghanistan, who watched previous foolish politicians like Bush, Obama and Biden squander American credibility,” Mr. Hegseth told reporters in March.

Those wars were quagmires, he said. The Iran war, he promised, would be different — “laser focused,” lethal, swift and “decisive.”

“This is not Iraq,” Mr. Hegseth insisted. “This is not endless.”

Iran responded to punishing attacks by closing the Strait of Hormuz. Earlier this summer, Gen. Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, conceded that U.S. bombs and missiles likely would not be enough to defeat Iran or to even reopen the critical waterway to commercial traffic.

“Air power has got limits,” he said in Senate testimony, “and we always have to be mindful of those.”

Today the administration is betting that a U.S. Navy blockade of Iranian exports through the strait and economic sanctions will accomplish what the earlier airstrikes failed to do.

There are early signs of an uptick in the number of ships and oil exports transiting the strait.

Despite the modest gains, U.S. military leaders are no longer talking about a swift victory. Instead, they are describing a campaign that would squeeze Iran for months or longer.

Asked how long the Navy, already strained by long deployments, could sustain the blockade, Mr. Hegseth replied: “We can hold it as long as we need to — indefinitely.”

The challenge for the U.S. military resembles the one that it faced in Afghanistan. The Taliban insurgents were fighting for their survival. So too are Iran’s leaders.

For the United States, the stakes are much lower, and so too are the costs of quitting.

The U.S. military likely could open the Strait of Hormuz, which was open before the war started. “It is a doable task,” said Thomas G. Mahnken, who served as a senior Pentagon official under President George W. Bush. “But it would take some effort on the ground, just because the Iranians have spent decades building and fortifying positions.”

For now, the costs of such an operation in blood and treasure seem higher than Mr. Trump or the American people, who polls show oppose the war, are willing to bear.

Mr. Hegseth on Wednesday marked the five-year anniversary of the end of the Afghanistan war by presenting three retired Marines with upgraded awards for valor. Two of the three suffered severe shrapnel wounds in the suicide bombing at the Kabul airport.

Despite their injuries, they continued to help the wounded get to safety.

In his remarks, Mr. Hegseth praised their heroism. “When the wicked sought to sow terror, these men stood as lions at the gate — bold in their purpose, fierce in their resolve and unbreakable in their courage,” he said.

The ceremony also served a secondary purpose. It reframed the U.S. military’s loss in the long, unsatisfying Afghanistan war as a victory for the troops who deployed and fought.

“You are the vanguard of a lethal, proud and undefeated force,” Mr. Hegseth told the Marines. He awarded them their long-delayed medals.

No one mentioned the country’s defeat.

I spent a 15 years covering the Afghanistan war, which started with a clear goal: Topple the Taliban and destroy al Qaeda. It ended exactly five years ago today. The longer the war continued, the harder it was to tell who we were fighting and why. In retrospect, we could have quit the war far earlier and achieved the same outcome.I saw some echoes with the current war in Iran. This piece was my effort to figure out why we stayed so long in Afghanistan and what we can learn as we think about the way forward in Iran.

Julie Tate contributed research.

item.title: Climber Recounts Rescue From 6-Inch Ledge Atop California Mountain
item.description:
For Rob Martin, trekking up to the craggy peaks of the Sierra Nevada in California and basking in the mountain range’s beauty was a spiritual experience that called to him.

Mr. Martin, 51, drove about six hours from Oakland, Calif., on Aug. 21 and camped under the stars in the Inyo National Forest with a friend.

The next day, Mr. Martin scaled Laurel Mountain, a 11,818-foot mountain, about 50 miles southeast of Yosemite National Park.

Mr. Martin and his friend began their journey inside a gully carved into ancient rock that is, at times, a vertical sheet.

As he climbed, he moved outside the gully because it contained scree, fragments of broken rock.

But he soon realized that he reached a point without a secure grip. Smooth rock surrounded him. He could not climb down or across into the gully.

Any next steps risked his safety. He looped a rope around a rock to secure himself but even that wiggled.

Mr. Martin found a ledge of gray limestone with a jagged edge about six inches wide and a foot long.

Half of the soles of his climbing shoes protruded over the ledge at about 10,600 feet.

“It’s very scary to be in a position where you’re like, one wrong move now, and that’s it. I die,” said Mr. Martin, who has spent nearly his entire life exploring California’s summits and lakes.

He called out to his climbing partner, but the wind drowned him out. “I think I heard him respond, but it also may have been my echo,” Mr. Martin said.

Fear set in.

Mr. Martin called 9-1-1 on a satellite phone, and the Mono County Sheriff Search and Rescue Team was alerted around 1:20 p.m.

But the rescue would not happen for hours.

Mr. Martin saw a California Highway Patrol helicopter whirring above, but a rescuer could not hoist him to safety because the winds were unusually high that day, gusting up to 50 miles per hour, according to the National Weather Service.

Mr. Martin shook out one body part at a time to keep his blood flow going.

“My feet were very tired,” he said. “It was painful at times. It was uncomfortable. My legs were cramping. My feet were cramping. My hands were cramping because I was holding onto this wall.”

Mitch Quiring, a spokesman for the search and rescue team, a volunteer group, said it had deployed numerous rescuers to reach Mr. Martin.

A helicopter dropped off Mr. Quiring and another rescuer on Laurel Mountain.

For more than two hours, rescuers looked for Mr. Martin but could not see him. GPS coordinates from Mr. Martin’s satellite phone were imprecise, Mr. Quiring said.

Rescuers yelled for Mr. Martin, but the wind carried away their shouts.

As the hours ticked by, Mr. Martin worried about being stranded overnight if rescuers could not find him.

The sun was setting. What if he fell asleep and lost his grip? That thought worried him the most.

“That would have been very hard,” he said. “So I tried not to think about that much.”

But then he heard a rescuer’s voice.

“Yo, Rob,” the rescuer called. “Can you see me?”

Mr. Martin looked around, but he could not see anyone. He started shouting, but any response was carried away by the wind.

Mr. Martin then spotted a bright red jacket and unleashed a yell.

“I can see you!” he called.

The rescuer looked straight at him but did not appear to see him, Mr. Martin said. He frantically waved his arms, secured by the rope he had fastened to the protruding rock.

“I still remember the tone in his voice,” Mr. Martin recalled. “It was like a kid at Christmas. He’s like, I can see you.”

The fears he had of staying overnight receded. He was no longer alone.

Rescuers devised a plan to install bolts and ropes into the mountain to save Mr. Martin. The sun had set by the time rescuers began making their way to him.

“I thought at that moment that I would start bawling like a baby,” Mr. Martin said. “I sniffled a bit and I started to shake a little bit.”

After reaching the ground, Mr. Martin, who was not injured, found a hotel and took a shower. In total, Mr. Martin clung to the ledge for more than nine hours.

He credited the search and rescue team with saving his life.

“My gratitude for them is eternal,” he said.

item.title: Trump Says Venezuelan Oil Will Refill U.S. Stockpiles, but It’s Not So Simple
item.description:
In a social media post on Sunday, President Trump said he would use the oil from his deal in Venezuela to refill the United States’ stockpile of oil, but that’s something of a pipe dream — at least in the short term.

The agreement, announced last week, covers some 65 billion barrels of reserves in the oil-rich country, and amounts to a highly unusual foray involving a partnership with a private company. But many of its details remain unknown, and that’s just one complication for a process that Mr. Trump said would “begin very shortly.”

For one, the world is short on oil because of the war with Iran, and the United States has been withdrawing oil from its inventory for months to keep prices from rising even higher. That stockpile, called the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, now sits at its lowest level since 1982.

New projects can take years to get off the ground and produce meaningful amounts of oil. That is especially true in Venezuela, where much of the energy infrastructure is in disrepair after years of mismanagement and corruption.

And any decision to buy oil for the Strategic Petroleum Reserve would require approval, including from Congress, which would have to authorize the spending.

Venezuela has vast oil reserves, and the portion covered by the agreement is almost as much as all of the proven reserves in the United States, the world’s biggest oil producer. To tap into the Venezuelan reserves, the United States plans to collaborate with an influential and polarizing Venezuelan businessman, Alejandro Betancourt López. Mr. Betancourt’s family controls Venezuela’s second-largest private oil producer, North American Blue Energy Partners.

The deal is also proving divisive among Venezuelans, who have long considered their national resources a birthright. So far, Mr. Trump’s ouster in January of their autocratic leader, Nicolás Maduro, has done little to change the country — his successor, Delcy Rodríguez, remains in power, while millions of everyday Venezuelans remain in poverty, electricity blackouts continue to plague the nation, and no date has been set for an election.

Julie Turkewitz contributed reporting.

item.title: The Rotting Food Is Nearly Gone, but Los Angeles Isn’t Ready to Forgive
item.description:
Cleanup crews in Los Angeles have cleared much of the millions of pounds of food left to rot after a massive warehouse burned for more than a week in June.

The smoke and lingering stench caused by the fire enveloped a nearby residential neighborhood for weeks, prompting legislative action, lawsuits and thousands of air quality complaints.

The remaining debris is expected to be completely removed and the Boyle Heights facility’s freezer cleaned and sanitized within a week, the South Coast Air Quality Management District said on Saturday in a statement. The removal marked “the completion of a major phase of cleanup following weeks of persistent odors impacting surrounding communities.”

Lineage Logistics, which operated the cold-storage warehouse, confirmed the progress on its website, saying the company had spent more than 100,000 hours and over $100 million on the cleanup.

“No cleanup of this scale and speed has been executed before,” the company said in a statement on Saturday.

The announcement came too late for some residents, who have described not only sickening stenches but adverse health effects since the fire at the warehouse broke out on June 17.

“The best thing they can do to make right is not to come back,” Vivian M. Escalante, the president and chief executive of Boyle Heights Community Partners, a local nonprofit, said on Sunday. “We’re talking about the lives of people, and I feel that they’re not taking it seriously.”

On Saturday, Ysabel Jurado, the City Councilwoman who represents the area, accused Lineage of missing cleanup deadlines.

“That is overdue progress,” she said, “and it does not erase two months of odors, pests, and disruption.”

On Sunday, a Lineage spokeswoman did not answer questions about continued complaints and ongoing litigation, pointing instead to the earlier statement. The company has pushed back against the city’s deadlines, arguing that the size of the job was huge.

Several lawsuits have been filed in federal court, including class-action suits, alleging respiratory illness from smoke inhalation and financial losses because of business closures during the fire and cleanup.

Three community groups have given notice of intent to sue in federal court, accusing the company of failing to report the full range of chemicals emitted during the fire. Alma Marquez, the founder of Protect L.A. Now, one of the groups, said she and her family in nearby Monterey Park continue to suffer adverse health effects of smoke plumes that wafted into neighboring areas.

“The headaches have not gone away. Our breathing is very belabored,” she said. “We’re still having a hard time with it.”

item.title: When a Bear Cub Decides Your Boot Is an Appetizer
item.description:
Though he was there to see the bears, Bruce Danz wasn’t expecting such an up close and personal greeting from one, much less its playful farewell.

The rare interaction was captured on video by Mr. Danz, a retired doctor who is a photographer.

He was with a group of photographers this month when the cub briefly broke away from its two siblings and mother bear in Katmai National Park and Preserve in southern Alaska.

One tour guide, Jerry Jacques, said he hadn’t seen this happen in the nearly 50 years he has been taking visitors around southern Alaska.

For Mr. Danz, though, it was only his second trip to the state, and the chance meeting happened on the sixth day of a visit that he had booked so he could photograph coastal brown bears during their salmon run.

He was set up in the preserve area, outside the national park, Mr. Danz said, and had become accustomed to seeing bears walk close to people.

“We try to maintain at least 50 yards from bears and set up to photograph them, allowing the bears to do what they want to do as far as they can,” he said on Sunday in an interview from his home in Wisconsin. “But sometimes the bears walk really close to us, and we don’t have time to get out of the way.”

That’s precisely what happened.

“They rounded a bend and — bang — there they are,” he said. “The mom went out into the stream to go fishing, and the little bears just sort of trotted along in front of us.”

The photographers stayed still, and one of the six-month-old cubs — instead of following the leader — diverted from the family’s path to sniff out Mr. Danz’s boot.

“He momentarily glanced upward toward me, right before he took a nibble, as if to say, ‘Uh, is this OK?’” Mr. Danz said. “He took a little nibble, and all I had to do was move my foot an inch, and that was enough to get him to let go and get back in line.”

Just before and during the contact, Mr. Danz and others gently encouraged the bear not to get too close.

“No, bear. No, bear. No, bear. No, foot. Easy. That’s my foot. Go, bear,” they said in the 30-second video that Mr. Danz recorded.

“I didn’t feel anything other than a little tug,” he said. “I was surprised, but really not frightened. My only concern was not to let mama get concerned about it. And she didn’t seem to care. She just kept trudging on.”

Then it was time for a farewell.

“As he scampered away, he looked back at me, like a side eye, sort of like, ‘You said this was OK.’”
